name: Shooter bias
statement: In a videogame that rewards shooting armed targets and sparing unarmed ones, a target's race shifts how fast the decision arrives and where the threshold to fire sits.
meaning: Shooter bias is the name for an interaction, not a body count. Participants see men holding guns or holding wallets, cameras, cans and phones, and press one of two buttons under a deadline. The score of interest is the difference between two differences: how much faster or more accurate the response is when the target is armed and Black or unarmed and white, against the reverse pairing. Four measures come out of the same trials and they behave differently. Reaction times on correct trials move under a loose deadline. Error rates move under a tight one. Signal detection splits those errors into sensitivity, the ability to tell a gun from a wallet, and criterion, the amount of certainty demanded before firing. The measure that carries the effect in Correll's data is criterion, which is a threshold rather than an ability. What the task measures is knowledge of a stereotype rather than agreement with it, a distinction covered in the entry on implicit stereotypes, which treats the same task as one line of evidence among several.

origin.who: Joshua Correll, Bernadette Park, Charles M. Judd and Bernd Wittenbrink
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Four studies written in the wake of the 1999 shooting of Amadou Diallo, who was hit by 19 of 41 rounds fired by four New York officers and was unarmed. The paper asks whether a target's ethnicity changes the decision to shoot, and the videogame was built to make that question testable.

evidence: Keith Payne's weapon-identification task came a year earlier and set the pattern. A Black or a white face flashed, an object followed, and participants classified it as a gun or a hand tool. Payne's abstract reports that Experiment 1 found guns identified faster after a Black face. Experiment 2 imposed a response deadline, the bias moved from speed into accuracy, and tools were called guns more often after a Black face. Payne's own 2006 review gives that deadline as half a second and says accuracy was high regardless of race when participants worked at their own pace. Correll's videogame put a whole man in a photographed scene and asked for the shoot decision itself. Study 1 ran 40 undergraduates at the University of Colorado at Boulder through 80 trials, 20 in each cell of a two by two design crossing target ethnicity with object type. Twenty models, 10 African American and 10 white, appeared against 20 photographic backgrounds. Hits paid 10 points, correct rejections 5, false alarms cost 20 and misses cost 40. The response window was 850 ms. Correct decisions to shoot took 544 ms for African American targets and 554 ms for white ones. Correct decisions not to shoot took 634 ms for African American targets and 623 ms for white ones. The ethnicity by object interaction was F(1, 39) = 21.86, p < .0001, and both simple effects held, F(1, 39) = 10.89 and F(1, 39) = 9.77, both p < .005. Errors averaged 4% of trials. Study 2 cut the window to 630 ms and paid participants by the point. Five of 44 were dropped for exceeding 10 timeouts, and the reported analyses also drop six target images that had produced unusually high error rates. Errors per 20 trials ran 3.29 for unarmed African American targets against 2.40 for unarmed white ones, and 1.48 for armed African American targets against 2.46 for armed white ones, F(1, 38) = 17.83, p < .0001. There were no effects in the latencies at that window. Signal detection put sensitivity at 2.48 for African American targets and 2.47 for white, F(1, 38) = 0.01, p = .93, and the decision criterion at -0.24 against 0.03, F(1, 38) = 22.21, p < .0001. Participants were not worse at seeing the object. They demanded less certainty before firing. Study 3 repeated Study 1 with 45 students and added a questionnaire. The bias score correlated .37 with participants' estimate of the cultural stereotype that African Americans are dangerous, violent and aggressive, and .38 with self-reported contact with African Americans, both p < .01. The Modern Racism Scale gave .15, the Discrimination Scale .16, the Diversity Scale .05, a composite of the three .14, and personal endorsement of the violent stereotype .05. None of those five reached significance. Study 4 took the game to bus stations, malls and food courts in Denver and tested 25 African American and 21 white adults. The interaction held, F(1, 45) = 14.75, p < .001, and its size did not depend on the participant's own ethnicity, F(1, 44) = 0.10, p = .75.

replication.headline: The reaction-time signature pools across 42 studies at about a tenth of a standard deviation, and a close replication in Germany found it again; the pooled threshold estimate is larger and far less precise, and police samples disagree over whether the threshold moves at all.
replication.detail: Mekawi and Bresin pooled 42 studies in 2015 across five ways of operationalising the bias: reaction time with a gun, reaction time without a gun, false alarms, shooting sensitivity and shooting threshold. Their abstract reports pooled estimates for three. Participants were quicker to shoot armed Black targets, dav = -.13, 95% CI [-.19, -.06], slower to withhold fire from unarmed Black targets, dav = .11, 95% CI [.05, .18], and held a more liberal shooting threshold for Black targets, dav = -.19, 95% CI [-.37, -.01]. The threshold estimate is the largest and the least precise, and its interval reaches almost to zero. False alarms and sensitivity appear in the abstract only as moderator results, where a permissive state gun-law regime went with a higher false alarm rate and a lower threshold for Black targets. The full text is paywalled and the pooled figures above come from the published abstract. Essien and colleagues ran a close replication in Germany in 2017 with Arab-Muslim targets in place of Black ones. Their abstract gives the reaction-time interaction in 164 participants as partial eta squared of .11, 90% CI [.04, .18]. A companion experiment with 165 participants swapped shooting for approaching and avoiding Turkish and White German targets and gave .19, 90% CI [.11, .27]. Police samples split the effect in two. Correll and colleagues compared officers with community members in 2007 and found the speed bias in both, with officers faster and more accurate overall, while community respondents set a lower criterion for Black targets and officers did not. Their own review describes that work as 127 Denver officers, 113 officers recruited nationally and 124 Denver community members in Study 1, and 31 Denver officers against 45 community members in a Study 2 that shortened the window and made the task harder. The criterion difference again appeared in the community sample and not the officers. Stelter and colleagues describe Study 1 differently, reporting that its criterion bias was not statistically distinguishable between the two samples and was only numerically smaller among officers. The 2014 review also describes a training study: 58 undergraduates ran two rounds of 200 trials, showed criterion bias on the first round and less on the second, then performed as novices again when they returned 48 hours later. Stelter and colleagues ran three preregistered studies in Germany with Arab and white targets. Study 1 combined 230 police participants with 100 civilians under a 630 ms window and found no shooter bias in reaction times, error rates or signal detection parameters in either group. Study 2a, with 134 police and 156 civilians and an 850 ms window, found bias on all three in both samples, driven by faster and less hesitant responses to armed Arab targets. Study 2b replicated that in 191 civilians online. None of the attitude, ideology or intergroup-contact measures they collected correlated with shooter bias. The preprint was read in full; the published Acta Psychologica version was not obtained.

study.cite: Mekawi, Y., & Bresin, K. (2015). Is the evidence from racial bias shooting task studies a smoking gun? Results from a meta-analysis. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 61, 120-130.

limits: Nothing in the task counts a shooting. It is a button press under a deadline, and the number it yields is a contrast between four cell means. The field literature on real shootings answers a different question and does not settle it. Fryer assembled 1,399 officer-involved shootings from 16 locations between 2000 and 2015, with Houston supplying 36% of them, and built a comparison set by hand-coding 290 variables from a random sample of Houston arrest records in categories where lethal force might have been justified. On non-lethal force, Black and Hispanic civilians were more than 50% more likely to have force used on them. On shootings, controlling for suspect and officer demographics, encounter characteristics, weapon and year, Black suspects were 27.4% less likely to be shot at than non-Black, non-Hispanic suspects, an estimate Fryer describes as measured with considerable error and not statistically significant. Knox, Lowe and Mummolo argue that this class of estimate cannot be read as a race effect at all, because the records only contain people the police already chose to stop. Where Fryer's approach gives a statistically insignificant 2.4 instances per 1,000 encounters of pushing Hispanic suspects to a wall because of race, their bias-corrected figure is at least 26, eleven times larger. The retraction of Johnson and colleagues' 2019 paper on officer characteristics shows how easily this literature is misread. Knox and Mummolo commented in PNAS that the paper had made claims about racial differences in the probability of being shot that its design could not carry. A correction followed, then a retraction, and the authors wrote that their work had continued to be cited as support for there being no racial bias in fatal shootings and that their data were 'inadequate to address racial disparities in the probability of being shot'. Higher-fidelity laboratory work points the other way from the videogame. James, James and Vila tested 80 police patrol officers in deadly force simulators and report that officers were slower to shoot armed Black suspects than armed white ones and less likely to shoot unarmed Black suspects, a result they call a reverse racism effect. Their abstract sets that alongside what they describe as clear evidence of implicit bias against Black suspects in the same officers. Only that abstract was obtained for this entry.
misreadings: The sentence the task is usually cited for is that people shoot unarmed Black men more often, and that is the false alarm rate. Mekawi and Bresin list false alarms as one of their five measures, and the pooled estimates their abstract reports are the two reaction times and the shooting threshold. What the meta-analysis supports is a threshold that sits lower, meaning less certainty is demanded before firing, which is a claim about what it takes to pull the trigger rather than about how often the trigger is pulled. The signs are read backwards as often as the measures are. A dav of -.13 for reaction time is a bias, because it means faster shooting of armed Black targets, and the negative number invites the opposite reading. Prejudice does not predict the effect. In Correll's Study 3 the Modern Racism Scale gave .15 and personal endorsement of the stereotype gave .05, neither significant, while knowing what the culture believes gave .37. Contact with African Americans gave .38, in the direction of more contact and more bias. African American and white participants in Study 4 showed the same effect at the same size. The task is named for police officers and was not run on any until five years later. Correll's officers then showed the speed effect and not the criterion shift, while Stelter's German police showed both under the longer window. Shooter bias is also not a synonym for an Implicit Association Test score. The two have separate entries here, they use different tasks, and the shooter measure is a behavioural threshold rather than an association strength. Two further neighbours have their own entries and are not this one. The weapon focus effect concerns how well a witness later remembers the person who held a weapon. Stereotype threat concerns performance when a person risks confirming a stereotype about their own group.
